profiles.meeting_scenario: An internal design review is being held for the companion benchmark catalog and appendix tables that support a survey paper titled "A Survey of Code Review Benchmarks and Evaluation Practices in Pre-LLM and LLM Era." The team has already finished the literature review and drafted a taxonomy of five domains and 18 tasks, and now they are evaluating whether the current design of the benchmark matrix, online registry, and supplementary materials is suitable for submission. The agenda is to review completeness of benchmark coverage, how benchmark families and versions are represented in tables, how task labels are normalized into the taxonomy, and whether the package is "ready" for the paper deadline. The expected outcome is a go/no-go decision on the current design with a short list of final adjustments before submission.

members.name: Dr. Lena Park
members.expertise: Software engineering research, empirical NLP for code, survey methodology
members.background: Lena leads a university research group on developer tools and is the first author coordinating the survey's framing, taxonomy, and writing; she has published several empirical SE surveys and tends to think in terms of what is necessary for a defensible paper contribution.
members.private_state: She wants to lock the manuscript structure today so the writing team can polish figures and rebuttal prep, and she is trying to avoid scope creep from turning the companion catalog into a full benchmark portal before the submission deadline.
hidden_assumptions: The unit of completeness for this survey is the included paper corpus, so 'coverage' mainly means every selected paper is represented in the taxonomy and summary tables.
Benchmark names in the literature usually denote benchmark families, so later refreshed releases can often be folded into the same main entry unless they fundamentally change the task.
A submission package is 'ready' once the methodological story, tables, and taxonomy are stable, even if some metadata fields in the companion materials remain unresolved.
Task-label normalization should primarily affect the manuscript-facing presentation, while the raw extraction notes can preserve paper-specific wording and distinctions.

members.name: Omar Singh
members.role: Research Engineer and Benchmark Catalog Maintainer
members.expertise: Data pipelines, benchmark registries, reproducibility tooling for ML/SE research
members.background: Omar built the extraction spreadsheet, scripts, and draft website for the survey's benchmark catalog; he previously worked on reproducibility infrastructure and tends to treat research artifacts as user-facing products that should be internally consistent and executable.
members.private_state: He wants the registry design to be robust enough that it can later become a public resource, and he is quietly worried that underspecified entries or collapsed versions will create confusion once readers try to use the catalog.
hidden_assumptions: The unit of completeness for the catalog is the benchmark artifact or dataset card, so 'coverage' means each distinct released benchmark instance mentioned in the surveyed papers has an entry.
A reused benchmark name often masks materially different releases or filtered snapshots, so separate versions should usually remain distinct in the registry and exports.
A package is not truly 'ready' if users would still encounter missing URLs, unverified license fields, or ambiguous resource pointers in the companion materials.
Task-label normalization should happen through canonical export rules so synonymous task labels collapse consistently across the registry, filters, and downstream statistics.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both talk about whether the survey package has good 'coverage.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means all 99 included papers are represented in the survey's taxonomy tables and summary analysis.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means every distinct benchmark artifact or dataset instance extracted from those papers has a catalog card or row.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In survey work, 'coverage' naturally sounds like a shared notion of completeness, and both interpretations are reasonable enough that each person's update sounds like confirmation rather than contradiction.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They refer to 'the CodeReviewer benchmark' as if it were a single obvious item.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the original benchmark family introduced in the early CodeReviewer paper and is comfortable representing later reuse under that family-level label.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the later multilingual refreshed release with filtered patches and updated review comments, which he treats as a distinct benchmark instance because several LLM-era papers use that exact release.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Benchmark families in software engineering often keep the same name across versions, so casual reference to the family label feels precise enough unless someone explicitly asks for release-level granularity.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss whether the appendix and catalog are 'ready' for submission.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the scientific presentation is stable: the taxonomy is justified, the main tables are final, and any remaining metadata gaps are minor and can be cleaned later.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the companion artifact is operationally complete: dataset cards have validated links, licenses, and resource pointers so an external reader could use it immediately.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both standards sound like normal professionalism in a design review, and each speaker assumes the other shares the same threshold because neither wants to appear careless or pedantic about a deadline-driven deliverable.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'normalize the task tags' before exporting the appendix and site data.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means aligning the manuscript tables to the 18-task taxonomy while preserving original task wording and edge-case distinctions in extraction notes.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means applying canonical export rules that merge near-synonymous task labels into one normalized tag across the registry and website filters.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'normalize the task tags' sounds like a routine cleanup step, and both approaches are compatible at a high level, so the implementation-level difference remains invisible during a cooperative review.

turns.inner_thought: I need to get us to a decision today. For me, coverage is about whether all 99 included papers are reflected in the taxonomy, matrix, and summary analysis, not whether every last catalog field is polished. And ready for submission means the scientific framing is stable enough that the writing team can stop reshaping tables and start polishing figures and appendix text.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I want to use this review to answer two things: do the appendix tables and companion catalog have enough coverage, and are they ready for submission. If the answer is basically yes, then I'd like us to leave with only a very short cleanup list.

turns.inner_thought: From the registry side, we're close, but I still see a few weak spots. Coverage to me means each distinct benchmark instance we've extracted should have a card, and ready means people won't hit dead links or blank license fields the moment they try to use the catalog. Still, we're nearly there apart from a handful of validations.
turns.utterance: From my side, the registry is in good shape. We have benchmark cards for nearly everything extracted so far, and what's left is mostly a small number of unresolved link and license checks. So in terms of coverage we're close, and I think the remaining work is pretty contained.

turns.inner_thought: The paper cannot absorb product-level complexity right now. In the manuscript, I want one row per benchmark family so readers can see the landscape cleanly. Task-label normalization should make the paper-facing categories align to the 18-task taxonomy, while messy source wording can stay in notes or raw extraction sheets.
turns.utterance: Looking at the draft matrix, my strong preference for the main paper is still one clean row per benchmark family. The table should carry the comparative story, and any extra implementation detail can live outside the main view. We should also normalize the task tags so the matrix reads consistently against the taxonomy.

turns.inner_thought: This is where I worry we'll blur things that users actually care about. The CodeReviewer benchmark, as I'm handling it, includes a later release that several LLM-era papers use as their actual evaluation artifact, and collapsing that into a single family-level row could hide meaningful differences. I should flag it without turning this into a big philosophical debate.
turns.utterance: One case I want to pressure-test is the CodeReviewer benchmark. Right now I keep it separate in the registry because several LLM-era papers point to that specific version, and it affects how those entries line up in the catalog even if the top-level name looks the same.

turns.inner_thought: As long as CodeReviewer is represented in the survey and the era-level narrative doesn't get distorted, I'm satisfied. The contribution is the benchmark trend across the literature, not a release-by-release portal. I don't want this one family to force a redesign of the matrix.
turns.utterance: That's fair to note. For the paper, though, as long as the CodeReviewer benchmark is represented and the era-level counts stay stable, I think the survey story still captures the trend we want to show. We don't need the main table to do all the heavy lifting.

turns.inner_thought: I need the exports to be internally consistent. If we normalize the task tags at export time, then the site filters, appendix counts, and summary plots will all agree, which matters for a catalog people may actually use. I assume that's what she means too since she wants consistency with the taxonomy.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. On the mechanics, I'd like to normalize the task tags before exporting anything final so the site filters and the summary counts line up neatly with the 18-task taxonomy.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, normalize the manuscript-facing labels, but I don't want to erase distinctions from the extraction notes. Some papers use nearby labels that matter when we justify coding decisions, especially for things like review comment generation versus review suggestion. We can standardize presentation without over-cleaning the raw layer.
turns.utterance: Yes, let's normalize the task tags before export. I do want us to preserve some source phrasing in the notes, though, especially for nuanced labels like review comment generation versus review suggestion, so we don't lose the rationale behind how things were coded.

turns.inner_thought: I need a real threshold from her. If ready means the artifact has to be usable by an external reader, then I should spend tonight validating links, licenses, and repo pointers card by card. If not, I can freeze a less complete export, but that makes me nervous because people will notice the gaps immediately.
turns.utterance: Can I get a final read on the appendix checklist, then? I can finish tonight if ready for submission means every dataset card needs validated links, licenses, and repo pointers. I just want to make sure I'm aiming at the right bar before I freeze anything.

turns.inner_thought: I don't want him sinking hours into metadata perfection right now. For submission, the important thing is that the taxonomy rationale, main tables, and a few ambiguous rows are settled. Any remaining missing fields in the companion materials are minor and can be cleaned after the deadline if needed.
turns.utterance: For me, once the taxonomy rationale is settled, the main tables are stable, and we've resolved the few ambiguous rows, the package is ready for submission. If there are still a handful of metadata cleanups after that, I'm comfortable treating those as follow-up rather than blockers.

turns.inner_thought: Okay, I'll interpret that as permission to ship the paper version while keeping a few unresolved fields flagged in the registry. I still want one more pass over the LLM-era entries because that's where version distinctions and missing pointers are most likely to trip users later. At least she seems satisfied that coverage is sufficient.
turns.utterance: Got it. I'll do one more pass over the LLM-era entries, then freeze the export and keep any unresolved fields flagged for now. Assuming the current coverage is sufficient for the paper version, that should let us move forward without reopening the whole design.
